articles.title: The U.S. May Be Approaching a Measles Crisis, and Some Babies Face Risks Before Birth
articles.description: Learn more about the recent rise in measles cases and how the virus is especially dangerous for newborns.

articles.title: 3D-printed scaffolds help turn waste methane into useful chemical using less power than liquid reactors
articles.description: When landfills and wastewater treatment plants create methane as a byproduct, much of it is simply burned and its value is lost. But the gas is an energy-rich resource that could be recycled as a fuel, chemical feedstock or bioproduct. Capturing and converting waste methane offers an opportunity to recover energy and create useful products from an otherwise wasted gas stream.

articles.title: Estimating suicide risk from text
articles.description: A new language-processing tool could help identify the highest-risk individuals from natural language, enabling swifter interventions.

articles.title: Michael Leon Receives Inaugural UC Regents Gamechanger Award for Memory Air
articles.description: Michael Leon, professor emeritus of neurobiology and behavior at the UC Irvine Charlie Dunlop School of Biological Sciences, received an inaugural Gamechanger Award.

articles.title: New findings explain how cells assemble machinery to repair damaged DNA
articles.description: A cell's ability to repair its damaged DNA is one of the most fundamental processes in biology, helping protect us from diseases like cancer. Over the years, researchers have unraveled many of the mechanisms cells use to repair DNA, ultimately leading to precision cancer treatments.

articles.title: Prison admissions rose 3% in district attorney election years during 'tough on crime' era
articles.description: New research from Northwestern Pritzker School of Law suggests that public sentiment associated with "tough on crime" politics may be tied to increases in the number of people admitted to state prisons during election years.

articles.title: People Are Already Lusting After Meta’s New AI Assistant Muse
articles.description: "some of y'all way too thirsty for muse," wrote Alexandr Wang, head of Meta's Superintelligence Labs, after posting a picture of its rear end. The post People Are Already Lusting After Meta’s New AI Assistant Muse appeared first on Futurism .

articles.title: AI-guided mutations help viruses infect bacteria up to 1 million times more effectively
articles.description: Biochemists at the University of Wisconsin–Madison are using AI to tackle one of modern medicine's most pressing challenges: the rise of antibiotic-resistant bacterial infections. Using data collected in their lab, biochemistry professor Vatsan Raman and his team built an AI model to identify new possibilities for fighting bacteria with one of their natural enemies. Their findings, published in the journal Cell Systems, could help accelerate the development of alternatives to traditional antibiotic drugs.

articles.title: Shared blueprint in aphid proteins helps AI predict their structures
articles.description: Tiny insects called aphids inject hundreds of mysterious proteins into plants, hijacking the plants' own genomes to build galls: structures made of plant tissue but constructed to the insects' specifications to house and feed their offspring.

articles.title: NASA to study human health and performance during Crew-13 mission
articles.description: During NASA's SpaceX Crew-13 mission aboard the International Space Station, astronauts will support a series of biomedical and human performance investigations, including a new collaborative effort to study how spaceflight affects blood flow and clotting. NASA also is testing crew members' manual piloting skills, evaluating methods to counter vision and brain changes, gathering essential health data to inform future missions, and measuring forces astronauts experience during their return to Earth to help refine re-entry hardware and procedures.

articles.title: First known case of Marfan syndrome discovered in feline siblings
articles.description: Researchers at the College of Veterinary Medicine and the Baker Institute of Animal Health have documented the first molecular characterization of Marfan syndrome, a rare inherited disorder that weakens connective tissues, in domestic cats.

articles.title: Without international law, ‘it’s my colleagues on the front line that get killed,’ says UN Relief Chief
articles.description: As the world faces mounting conflicts and crises, UN Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs Tom Fletcher tells Christiane Amanpour about the decisive action world leaders at the UN General Assembly can take to help millions across the globe.

articles.title: 'They wouldn't say it in person': Young gamers reveal their personal experiences in online multiplayer gaming
articles.description: A new UEL research project is exploring practical ways to reduce antisocial and harmful behavior in online gaming while helping platforms create more positive and inclusive experiences for young players.

articles.title: New species of proto-amphibian described by students, named in honor of their mothers
articles.description: Around 309 million years ago, long before the dinosaurs, the area around Chicago was a swampy river delta swarming with early land-dwelling animals, giant insects and strange swimming animals. What was once a hotbed for new forms of life to flourish and evolve has become one of today's richest Carboniferous period fossil deposits. Two student scientists from the Field Museum have just described the latest animal discovered at this location—and they named it after their mothers, who both happen to be named Jean.

articles.title: From research to impact: Yale’s Tobin Center drives work that shapes policy and improves lives
articles.description: In a new impact report, Yale’s Tobin Center for Economic Policy’s documents its work to reduce the time between top-flight research and policy impact.

articles.title: U.S. AI infrastructure buildout is surpassing every prior investment in American history
articles.description: A Brookings Institution study projects $10.3 trillion in AI data center investment through 2032, exceeding prior buildouts as a share of GDP

articles.title: Stanford Scientists Find That the Human Brain Is Actually Two Separate Organs
articles.description: "I was surprised at our findings because the word 'brain' implies a contiguous organ that likely has a singular origin." The post Stanford Scientists Find That the Human Brain Is Actually Two Separate Organs appeared first on Futurism .

articles.title: Unlike many parents, children are fearless around AI
articles.description: Researchers in UC's College of Arts and Sciences spoke to 41 children ages 5 to 10 after inviting them to play three interactive games with Miko, a commercially available robot that uses generative AI.

articles.title: Aardwolves and cats share surprising chromosome similarities
articles.description: In the first detailed chromosome map of the aardwolf, Texas A&M University researchers have discovered that, despite millions of years of separate evolution, the chromosomes of aardwolves, other hyenas and even domestic cats have remained remarkably similar.

articles.title: US tech drives European nuclear reactor to ditch weapons-grade uranium fuel
articles.description: Belgium's SCK CEN has asked regulators to approve converting the BR2 research reactor to low-enriched uranium.

articles.title: The Ovary Is Surprisingly Active After Menopause. Scientists Are Trying to Figure Out Why
articles.description: A growing body of research is putting the ovary in a new light, not as an egg factory with an expiration date, but as an organ that shapes women’s health long after the fertile years have passed.

articles.title: STAT+: Why Gilead can’t stop talking about its ambitions in immunology
articles.description: Gilead Sciences’ top executives have been emphatically bullish about the biotech’s years-long push to develop drugs for inflammatory and autoimmune diseases.

articles.title: Why This Weekend’s Nor’easter Is Like a Hurricane
articles.description: Nor’easters are usually a winter phenomenon. But this week’s storm is arriving earlier than usual, and it could take on some characteristics more typical of tropical systems.

articles.title: Stanford Engineers Teach Spacecraft to "Dream" Their Way to the Space Station
articles.description: Docking with the ISS may seem simple. However, actually doing so is a showcase in how difficult orbital mechanics can be. It’s equivalent to traveling down a highway at 28,000 km/hr and parallel parking into an open garage on a multi-billion dollar laboratory traveling at the same speed. If you try to accelerate forward you actually drift up, and there’s no air friction to naturally slow you down. Oh, and if you hit the lab, everyone onboard both your craft and the station dies, and the resultant debris field could both wipe out dozens of satellites and even people on the ground. No pressure, obviously. For decades, aerospace engineers have been docking successfully using hard coded physics equations and human pilots to correct them. But now, a new paper, available in pre-print on arXiv from researchers at Stanford, is taking a shot at building an AI to perform a series of “mental simulations” that could fundamentally change how future spacecraft interact with each other.

articles.title: Meta launches an 'evil Tamagotchi': Muse Charm gadget lets you use AI without your phone or computer
articles.description: The futuristic device, called Muse Charm, was announced by Meta's CEO, Mark Zuckerberg, at the end of the Meta Connect event last night.

articles.title: IFR Counts 7,000 Humanoid Robot Sales as Workplace Pilots Stay Small
articles.description: IFR counted about 7,000 humanoid robot sales in 2025, but many units remain in research and workplace pilots rather than productive commercial roles. The post IFR Counts 7,000 Humanoid Robot Sales as Workplace Pilots Stay Small appeared first on TechRepublic .

articles.title: Engineering the Substation Exit for Reliability, Capacity, and Expansion
articles.description: This white paper gives distribution engineers and utility teams a practical overview of the substation exit, the short and high-consequence section where station capacity divides into individual feeders. It explains how covered, spacer-supported overhead construction can reduce common contact-driven faults while leaving room for future circuits. What you will learn about: Why a fault near the substation exposes more customers than one farther along the feeder, and why the first spans out of the station carry so much reliability weight. How covered conductors and spacer-cable systems differ from bare overhead conductors, and why covered conductor is not treated as touch-safe insulation. Which engineering factors shape a sound exit design, including conductor rating, protection coordination, grounding, and structural loading. How overhead spacer cable compares with conventional bare overhead and underground shielded cable across footprint, reliability, and lifecycle cost. How to move a project from concept to commissioning using staged design gates and a clear performance specification. Download this free whitepaper now!

articles.title: Could comet 3I/ATLAS teach us about life beyond Earth? Scientists say the story's not over yet.
articles.description: No evidence has been found linking 3I/ATLAS to aliens. But the interstellar object, just the third of its kind to be found, shows that life's molecular precursors are abundant in the Milky Way.

articles.title: No synagogues, but signs of fishing 20,000 years ago in northern Israel
articles.description: Why the obsession with biblical archaeology? On the banks of what is now the Jordan River, Gonen Sharon finds evidence relevant to all humanity

articles.title: Venus May Have Devoured Its Moon
articles.description: One of the great mysteries in astronomy has been why Venus has no moon. Now a new theory provides a simple answer: It might have been eaten.

articles.title: Aerial maps reveal successful woodland expansion in Scotland's Cairngorms
articles.description: A University of Cambridge–led team has used aerial surveys across a huge swath of the Cairngorms National Park in Scotland to create detailed 3D maps that show the beginnings of large-scale recovery of native woodland.

articles.title: Carly Rae Jepsen works round-the-clock in Day and Night
articles.description: Music history is full of excellent releases made in the wake of new motherhood - from Lauryn Hill's Miseducation to Eartheater's Heavenly Body this year. Carly Rae Jepsen has a habit of releasing albums in two, typically releasing a B-side album for each cycle. These storied traditions came together on Sept. 18 for Day and Night , the pop star's eighth studio release and first double album arriving right after the birth of her first child. While not quite her Ray of Light , this outing features a tremendous expansion of Jepsen's sonic palette and some more feathers in the cap of contemporary pop's most consistent should've-been-a-hit-maker. With 24 songs for 24 hours, the album is split into 'day' and 'night' sides. The Day side songs share an autumnal wistfulness with a focus on live instrumentals Jepsen hasn't spotlighted so strongly since her debut . The Night side gives her classic synthpop a clubbier spin. There's no doubt Jepsen had little difficulty filling up 84 minutes - fans will recall her claims of writing 200 songs for Dedicated . The diverse production choices help the time go by quickly, but I question the inclusion of some of these tracks (' That's Just Me " goes in one ear and out the other). The album's singles are well selected for the most part. " On Wires " and " After All " mark the public's introduction to the album's day side, and both remain among the strongest tracks on the record. The emphatic guitar-driven chorus of "On Wires" (with the classic Jepsen brass in the back of the mix) marks a radical departure from her typical sound. Meanwhile, "After All," a soulful and hazy fall-time picture of family life, opens the album as a natural evolution of the disco sounds from her previous The Loveliest Time . The Night side was represented in the singles department by " Don't Leave Me on the Dancefloor ," which evokes ABBA in its bright piano keys and Robyn's patent ' sad banger ' style. " Motivation " marks well-explored territory as a catchy, almost embarrassingly sincere dance-pop ode to found family. The single " Versailles ," released alongside the album, is perhaps most telling for Jepsen's intentions with her latest project. Stuttering piano appears and disappears as she switches in and out of a slower, ballad-esque tempo and a dance track to dissolve in. These adventurous production choices crop up in several other tracks, from the mild psychedelic distortions in " Something Tragic " to the closer of the Day side, " Just a Little Walk on the Moon ." Her vocals in the bossa nova influenced song sound like they're emerging from an evening radio, as the album prepares for the night side of life. " Gimme your time, gimme your nights, gimme your days " she demands on " Habits of Creatures " - and who can deny her? Jepsen's B-sides do tend to have the better songs - I staunchly maintain both Dedicated: Side B and The Loveliest Time are superior to their A-side counterparts - and this double album does not mark an exception. While the stripped back and instrument-based soundscape of the Day side do not always synergise with the pop star's strengths, her forays into new dancefloor territory on the Night side yield more consistently magical results. " Never Let a Good Thing Die " immediately launches listeners from the Day side into the club, pulsating with jittery beats before expertly transitioning into an expansive outro. Right after, " Amalfi Coast " recalls Jessie Ware's nu-disco while blending a vocoder and synth to glorious house effect. Jepsen does not stray far from her usual lyrical grounds across the album, but in " Patience Power Passion " she delights in the irresistible bounce of the chorus , while in " Diver " she pulls out enough metaphors to please a high school English teacher. Her warehouse of dance references expands with the build-up to the garage-style beat of " Near or Far ," merging with her poppy sensibilities where " No Labels, I Love You " conjures up classic house for everyone to get up and dance. Fittingly, she draws the curtains on " Super Sage ," an ethereal and enveloping track filled with love. Day and Night is among Jepsen's more mellow and less immediate records, along the tone of The Loneliest Time . It is also perhaps her most ambitious album so far - released during one of the busiest periods of her life (keep an ear out for her upcoming 10 Things I Hate About You musical ). "My joke is that I'm at some point going to write a memoir, and it'll be called The Year We Did Everything at Once, " she described in an interview with Elle . For an album which reflects this breadth, all of it - the new, the familiar, the great, the less-good - feels at home in the sonic world she has constructed in her musicianship. This stylistic expansion is a new springboard to continue growing her flawless discography (yes, including Tug of War ). As the world of dance-pop evolves, Carly Rae Jepsen strengthens her niche and keeps her loyal listeners excited to run away with her once more.

articles.title: 'Researcher of the Year' to be sacked as part of cost cutting
articles.description: Not even the Premier's STEM Researcher of the Year 2025 can avoid a Tasmanian departmental job-cutting drive.

articles.title: Strange Galaxies in the Early Universe Were Shaped by Weird Stars
articles.description: Galaxies and their stars in the early Universe look a lot weirder than those we see today, and astronomers want to know why. A team of researchers at the University of Utah decided to survey certain stars in nearby galaxies as analogs of those that existed when the Universe was still in its infancy. The survey, called the "Treasury of Extremely Metal-Poor O Stars (TEMPOS), used the ultraviolet (UV) light streaming from those relatively close-by stars as detected by the Hubble Space Telescope's Cosmic Origins Spectrograph.

articles.title: In House primaries, organized groups may matter more than voters
articles.description: In most of the nation's 435 congressional districts, the general election is not much of a contest. With the vast majority of U.S. House seats considered safe for one party or the other, the primary usually determines who goes to Congress—and it is the election Americans know the least about. A new book co-authored by a researcher at the Annenberg Public Policy Center (APPC) of the University of Pennsylvania finds that voters are rarely the most important influence on the outcome.

articles.title: Acute hunger could reach 8 million children in six African countries as El Niño looms
articles.description: About 8 million children across East and Southern Africa could face acute hunger by early 2027, a rise of 30%, as one of the strongest El Niño weather events in recent years fuels a growing food crisis, according to a new analysis by Save the Children.

articles.title: New Lunar Crater Offers Keys To Moon’s Shallow Subsurface
articles.description: Asteroids which strike the Moon and create new craters offer lunar scientists a window onto the workings of our natural satellite’s shallow subsurface.

articles.title: Across southwest China and Thailand, plant turnover and nematode body width help explain soil diversity
articles.description: Soils harbor some of the most diverse life on Earth. Soil nematodes play crucial roles in maintaining ecosystem functions. Yet how their diversity changes across large landscapes, and what drives those changes, remains poorly understood.

articles.title: Circle au symposium Autonomous 2026 : le lancement d’Arc suscite l’intérêt
What joining the EU's Erasmus+ program could mean for Canada
articles.description: In his recent address to the European Parliament, Prime Minister Mark Carney proposed that Canada join Erasmus+, a European Union program that supports education, training, youth and sports.

articles.title: Ancient genome function persists despite frequent mutations, centromere study shows
articles.description: Every time a cell divides, its chromosomes must be distributed correctly between the two daughter cells. Central to this process is the centromere, a specialized region of the chromosome. The centromere serves as the attachment site for the cellular machinery that pulls the chromosomes apart.

articles.title: Software Update Turns Samsung’s “AI Fridges” Into Useless Bricks
articles.description: Wait, why did fridges need AI in the first place? The post Software Update Turns Samsung’s “AI Fridges” Into Useless Bricks appeared first on Futurism .

articles.title: Scientists build world's most accurate atomic clock
articles.description: Take a second and turn it into trillions of moments. Measure each one. That's how precisely an atomic clock at Singapore's Centre for Quantum Technologies (CQT) keeps time—and with record-setting accuracy, according to results published in Nature on Sept. 23.

articles.title: Fluorescence timing identifies eight proteins in one cell with a single staining step
articles.description: An international collaboration led by the University Medical Center Göttingen (UMG), Germany, has developed a labeling method that distinguishes fluorescent labels not by color but by how long it takes a dye to emit fluorescence. This makes it possible to visualize eight different proteins in a cell simultaneously in a single step using standard microscopes. The results have been published in the journal ACS Nano.

articles.title: Political shifts may shape how quickly Germany adopts electric cars and solar power
articles.description: A new study conducted by the Climate Action Research Lab (CARL) at the University of Freiburg finds that electric cars and photovoltaic systems are less widespread on average in municipalities with strong support for Alternative for Germany (AfD). The researchers also examined how changes in political support within the same municipalities over time affect subsequent adoption of these technologies. They found that an increase in the AfD's share of the vote is followed by relatively slower adoption of electric cars and photovoltaic systems. The technologies continue to spread, but at a slower rate. The work is published in the journal Nature Sustainability.

articles.title: 240-Million-Year-Old Fossil Turns Out to Be a New Species That Could Rewrite Dinosaur Evolution
articles.description: Learn more about the newly identified species Dinodontosaurus isiyavamanda and how its discovery could reshape scientists' understanding of the timeline of dinosaur origins.

articles.title: Researchers create ultra-tiny OLED with UV-printed pixels, just like microchips
articles.description: ETH Zurich researchers have developed light-emitting OLED polymers that can survive photolithography, potentially allowing tiny pixels to be patterned with chipmaking precision. The breakthrough could pave the way for ultra-small, high-resolution displays for AR glasses and tiny light sources for medical research, sensors and microscopy.
